Space Cat Felicette

Félicette, a small French cat, made history as the first feline to travel to space on October 18, 1963. Launched by France’s space program aboard a Véronique rocket, she reached an altitude of about 100 miles.

Equipped with electrodes to monitor her vital signs, Félicette endured a 15-minute suborbital flight, experiencing weightlessness briefly before safely parachuting back to Earth. Her mission provided valuable data on the effects of space travel on living organisms. Sadly, though she returned safely to Earth, she was later euthanised for subsequent scientific study.

Félicette was honored with a statue in 2019, celebrating her pioneering role in space exploration.

#OnThisDay in 1916, Perce Blackborow, Welsh sailor and famed polar stowaway aboard Shackleton's expedition ship 'Endurance', underwent surgery on Elephant Island to amputate his frostbitten and gangrenous toes.

In 1914 Blackborow and his friend William Blakewell, found themselves in Buenos Aires without a ship. When 'Endurance' arrived in port and two of the crew were sacked, the pair thought their problems were solved. Shackleton interviewed them both and whilst Blakewell was accepted, Blackborow was not, due to his age and lack of experience. With Blakewell's help he was smuggled on board and was eventually discovered three days into the journey.

Despite being unhappy to find the stowaway, Shackleton had no option other than to keep him on board and offered him a steward position. Nicknamed 'Blackie', Blackborow proved to be clever, conscientious and popular with the crew.

On the lifeboat journey from where the 'Endurance' sank to Elephant Island, Blackborow made the mistake of wearing leather rather than the cold weather felt boots that the other men wore, and he developed frostbite in his toes which turned gangrenous. When they arrived at the island, he had to crawl through the surf to reach land and shortly afterwards underwent the surgery which removed all the toes of his left foot.

In the accompanying image, Blackborow is photographed with the cat of Henry McNish the ship's carpenter. Named Mrs Chippy, after the traditional nickname for a carpenter, the cat quickly became the ships mascot.

📸 Perce Blackborow with Mrs Chippy. Frank Hurley, SPRI.

Nitama, the calico cat who served as the second-ever feline stationmaster of Wakayama Electric Railway’s Kishigawa Line, was honoured with a funeral at her home station in Japan’s Wakayama Prefecture on 13 December.

The railway company said Nitama passed away on 20 November after falling ill in late October. Around 500 people, including railway staff and devoted fans, gathered at Kishi Station to pay their respects, as the company formally enshrined her and posthumously conferred the title of “Honorary Special Stationmaster.”

Nitama took over the beloved role in 2015 following the death of Tama, the iconic first feline stationmaster whose appointment helped revive the once struggling local rail line.

The strange story of Oscar, the therapy cat.

In 2005, a peculiar case emerged from a US nursing home, when Oscar, a six-month-old kitten, was introduced as a therapy cat. 

Unlike typical therapy animals, Oscar demonstrated an uncanny ability to predict the imminent passing of residents. His penchant for solitude was interrupted by moments of profound connection when he would deliberately choose to lie beside specific individuals. Strangely enough, those chosen few died within a mere few hours.

At first, workers in the nursing home didn't notice anything weird, but after it happened 20 times, they started to found a link: Oscar clearly knew when someone would going to die. 

The story of Oscar prompts a crucial question: can felines genuinely sense the approach of death in humans? While the scientific community is in the early stages of unraveling the mysteries behind such phenomena, preliminary findings suggest that animals might indeed pick up on subtle cues, such as changes in scent or behavior, that precede an individual's demise.

Oscar passed away in 2022 after being right about more than 100 deaths during his life.

Source:

Dosa, D. (2007). A Day in the Life of Oscar the Cat. New England  Journal of Medicine, 357(4), 328-329. doi: 10.1056/NEJMp078108

The cat seen in Caught Stealing (2025) is actually Tonic, a Siberian Forest Cat, his owner and lead trainer, Melissa Millett, found him as a stray kitten wandering the streets of Toronto about 8 years ago.

Tonic was known for his extreme focus, once staying on his "mark" for an hour and a half. However, if he didn't feel like doing a take after 10 or 12 rounds, he would simply refuse to get back on his mark, signaling he was "done" for the day

To prepare for the film's intense scenes, Millett practiced "fake killing" her assistant in front of Tonic so he would stay calm during the movie's bone-crunching violence. 

Before this film, Tonic already had a "horror icon" resume. He played the pre-death version of Church in the 2019 Pet Sematary remake and also appeared as Dewey in the 2023 slasher Thanksgiving.

Director Darren Aronofsky admitted he is a dedicated "dog person" and generally "hated cats" before production. After working with Tonic, he was so impressed that he said he’d "work with Tonic in a second again over many human actors".

The Hidden Design Genius Behind Japan’s Most Trusted Delivery Logo.

Japanese designer Kenya Hara, through Nippon Design Center, led the 2021 refinement of Yamato Transport’s iconic Kuroneko mark, the first redesign of the symbol in 64 years. The story, however, begins in 1957, when Yamato founder Yasuomi Ogura was inspired by the mother-and-kitten emblem of American transport company Allied Van Lines, whose idea of “careful handling” resonated with Yamato’s approach to delivery. Ogura obtained permission to use the concept, and Yamato’s own mark was designed by Takeshi Shimizu, who worked in the company’s public relations department. There is an especially charming detail behind its creation: Shimizu’s young daughter drew the family’s black cat, Kuro, on a sheet of paper using crayons.

Her drawing of the mother cat and kittens became an important inspiration for the final symbol. Remarkably, in 2016 another cat drawing was discovered on the back of the same sheet, showing a kitten positioned at its mother’s mouth, an image even closer to the eventual logo. In 2021, Hara refined the symbol without changing its essential character, carefully examining details such as the eyes and ears and replacing the traditional outlined oval with a softer, more expansive ellipse. The result modernised a 64-year-old symbol while preserving its enduring message of care, reassurance and trust.
